items.body:
All upward lift and kosmiche synth iridescence from Seoul’s blissed family band, back on the Far East’s leading krautrock revival label, Guruguru Brain...

“The blissed family band is back! TENGGER have always moved together, through time, space & genre. 'SKY' arrives as a new chapter: a little more still, a little more inward, while keeping all the warmth that's always been at the heart of what they do.

Embodying the band name meaning "endless sky" in Mongolian and "vast sea" in Hungarian, their 8th album 'SKY' centres on the feelings of boundless, infinite expansion. Conceived as one continuous environment rather than a collection of tracks, the album unfolds slowly through luminous synths, patient drones and Itta's breath-like vocals.

Like a soft big sky you can actually float on: 'SKY' is vast, warm, and wide open.

"Rather than a specific emotion, we hope the record opens a certain awareness — that the sky is not just something to be seen. Through it, we sense a connection to something much larger — a feeling of being linked to the wider universe. This sense of connection runs through the entire record.””

items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.

"This album is created over the past years with my brother Alfred. This period has been spiritually transformative for me. it reflects the playfulness and authenticity that com
items.body:
Custom-built for sunny days, Sofie Birch’s solo Stroom debut melds bossa and psych pops with delicate touches of 4th world ambient jazz and chamber music in a chiffon-layered, naïf dream sequence landing somewhere on the line between Sam Prekop's self-titled alltimer, Antena's Camino Del Sol x Stereolab on the downbeat...

"This album is created over the past years with my brother Alfred. This period has been spiritually transformative for me. it reflects the playfulness and authenticity that comes out of releasing deep traumas and healing wounds. this music comes from a deep place of joy and connection with my brother and with the essense of being a child. being filter free and in contact with the most uncomplicated and loving parts of ourselves, still emphasizing magic and mystery, like childhood does without asking for permission or confirmation.

It took me a while to actually see the music as an interconnected piece. i have been taking in and out material, re mixing, removing, rearranging, re producing and regretting all along the way. but suddenly when we mastered this selection on a cassette tape recorder, the meaning started to reveal itself and drawing threads back in time.

Bivabippalukka is playfulness, intuition, transition and myths. the page of cups. the ideas rising, the energy flowing, flowers, stars and jumping creatures on the verge of dimensions. fortune telling, magic cards, secret caves and things that disappear right in front of you. many talented guests playing with me and my visions on the album.

Bossa nova is the most comforting genre for me. and we need comfort in these times. we need comfort to heal and feel joy to be able to keep dreaming and manifesting - and transmuting the world.

I am not gonna play this music live in the form it appears. i will still continue playing spiritual ambient music. this work is something else. it is pocket of joy, a cup with a fish. it is a step on the journey, like everything else."

Active since ’89, the rotating assembly of Pablo’s Eye, headed by Axel Libeert, have plotted a unique course thru the backwaters of art rock, ambient, fantasy soundtrack music, and whatever else they fancy, leading to a pair of retrospectives on Stroom in 2018-19, plus the cult E
items.body:
The Mitteleuropa enigma is strong on the 2nd original LP by Pablo’s Eye for Stroom, commanding attention to noctilucent, cinematic synth scapes laced with hand-played drums and poetry that plays out like a waking dream.

Active since ’89, the rotating assembly of Pablo’s Eye, headed by Axel Libeert, have plotted a unique course thru the backwaters of art rock, ambient, fantasy soundtrack music, and whatever else they fancy, leading to a pair of retrospectives on Stroom in 2018-19, plus the cult EP ‘Bardo For Pablo’, and fresh material on ‘The Light Was Sharp, Our Eyes Were Closed’ (2024).

Here represented by Marie Mandi, Luc Laret, Thierry Royo, Richard Skinner, Axel Libeert, and Ludwig Lapauw on ‘Everything You Give Away’, they follow noses for a typically low slung and resoundingly atmospheric album primed to seduce anyone in its path, as they stealthily proceed from the nightfall of ‘Walking the Line’, reminding us of DAAC, to the blushed choral pads and trip hop bass of ‘Reverie’ and Reese bass-gilded centrepiece ‘A dash of raspberry’, and ultimately the widescreen departure of ‘October ’75’. 

Trés classy.

items.body:
Munich’s modern art gallery Museum Brandhorst field wide ranging responses to an exhibit of works and concerts focussed on the works of John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg and Cy Twombly, ranging from the sound poetry of Sofia Biazzi; to the sublime levitations of Maria Margolina; avant ambient pop of water lily; the pulsating technoid attack of focus baby; andCaroline Kretschmer’s subaquatic intrigue.

“Museum Brandhorst has invited Sound and Experiment to create a series of performances, audio works, and concerts in relation to the exhibition Fünf Freunde: John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly. The event took place on June 27, 2025, as part of the Junge Nacht and the opening night of the annual Kunstareal Fest in Munich. The program featured newly produced pieces by Sound and Experiment participants Sofian Biazzi, Ilinca Fechete, focus baby, Daniel Gianfranceschi, Bruno Haas, Caroline Kretschmer, Bradley Leonard, Camilla Metelka, Maria Margolina, rosi and water lily. 

In a preparatory, biweekly seminar, discussions addressed conditions such as spectrotemporal displays, sharing time and frequency domains with different sound pieces simultaneously, and eventual performance constellations. An additional point of departure was a close reading of the indirect role of American artist David Tudor in some of the positions exhibited in Fünf Freunde, the function of the organization E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology), and auditory scene analysis and synthesis in general.

The pieces featured on this CD are related to the presented performances, yet newly produced and with the audio CD format in mind.”

items.body:
Anyone obsessed with those two incredible ‘Begena Songs…’ comps on Death Is Not The End will be properly enchanted by this more expansive - yet still intimate - suite of snapshots from Ethiopia, 1971, spanning the unique, twanging harp sound thru to Amharic poetry, chants, and spellbinding flute dances...

One that catches the breath with seldom felt sensations, ‘Ethiopian Musics 1971’ patently owes as much to the incredible performers as their faithful representation in Ragnar Johnson & Ralph Harrisson’s recordings. All secreted to tape on a Uher Report L stereo reel-to-reel recorder, they epitomise an era of ethnomusicological preservation, when the likes of labels such as Lyrichord and  Folkways were already decades deep “in the field”, documenting long-held traditions practically untouched by an encroaching, western modernity. And perhaps most crucially, the recordings beautifully render the acoustic settings and vivid vibes with an immersive quality in stark opposition to the era of dry, so-called audiophile studio recordings of ethnic musics to come - all the better for immersing in this wonderfully unfamiliar world.

The abundance of singular tones and strong, rare feels they produce is quite staggering to our northern english ears, and we reckon also for anyone else, for that matter. Opening to a joyful couplet of a bluesy ’Song about the beauty of women’, and the almost shanty-like swing and hard rhythm of ’Tej Beit Song’, the set reels to distinctive pieces of Ethiopian Christian song set to begena, or ‘Harp of David’, buzz, and a landscape-scale, 13 minute ‘Love Song (Mary Armede)’. A gripping ‘Drum Song (Jigsaw)’ will be mana to rhythm fiends, and a number of standout flute pieces reprise the frisson of our first encounter with this discipline on Sublime Freq’s ‘Staring into the Sun - Ethiopian Tribal Music’ set of 2012, most potently on the pluming twin pipes of the ‘Fila Flute Dance’ parts, whilst the pentatonic craar (6-stringed lyre) parts surely strike nerves for lovers of the rawest blues, and hail the liberated legacy of Mary Armede, a folk singer-fashion designer of Azmari heritage who surely warrants further investigation. 

No doubt this is one of the most striking archival discoveries of 2026, acutely advised to anyone enchanted with music from this corner of the world from Éthiopiques to begena harp, thru to Ragnar Johnson’s other arenas of research for Ideologic Organ in Yemen or Papua New Guinea. Dive in without delay.

items.body:
Mu-inspired space cadets KiF Productions livicate their play of Japanese environmental ambient electronics, Hassellian 4th world, the KLF’s ‘Chill Out’, and Eno-esque harmonic perfumes, to the dearly departed Keith McIvor​.

"Passiflora (Passifloraceae) is a genus of around 550 species of flowering plants, native to the tropical and subtropical Americas. The Passion Flower is a plant of improbable beauty - its blooms almost too intricate to be real, its climbing habit a quiet kind of determination. It has been used for centuries as a remedy for anxiety and sleeplessness, something that slows us and the world around us down.

Fresh from last year's triumphant debut by KiF; Still Out, Passiflora, the album, follows the plant from its very beginning. It opens in darkness - 'Secret of the Seed', dormant, waiting - before the first tentative stir of 'First Movement' and the long, instinctive reach of 'Seeking Light'. From there, the journey unfolds with the patience of something that has no choice but to grow: drinking, climbing, flowering. 'Song of the Vine' carries the plant's quiet insistence upward, while 'Florescence' and 'Pollination Dream' catch it at its most open - that brief, extraordinary moment of full bloom. Then the turn. 'Fruiting (Slight Return)' and finally 'Return to Earth' - the cycle completing itself, giving back what it always borrowed.

Each track is a stage. The whole is a life cycle."

items.album: Around Here, The Birds Plant The Trees
items.excerpt: Ambient composer Natalia Beylis leads an ensemble of Nyahh’s finest in her landscape-shaped evocation of a field in Leitrim, Éire, quietly meditating on the natural logic of birds and trees. ‘Around Here The Birds Plant The Trees’ is Beylis’ slow-burn, long-form arrangement for quintet - Eimear Reidy (cello), Tola Custy (fiddle), Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh & Ultan O’Brien (violin), and Willie Stewart (percussion) - seeded in her reading of a blackbird’s dawn chorus, and subsequent conversation with
items.body:
Ambient composer Natalia Beylis leads an ensemble of Nyahh’s finest in her landscape-shaped evocation of a field in Leitrim, Éire, quietly meditating on the natural logic of birds and trees.

‘Around Here The Birds Plant The Trees’ is Beylis’ slow-burn, long-form arrangement for quintet - Eimear Reidy (cello), Tola Custy (fiddle), Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh & Ultan O’Brien (violin), and Willie Stewart (percussion) - seeded in her reading of a blackbird’s dawn chorus, and subsequent conversation with a local farmer on how “birds are the architects of the living landscape”. It follows some 40 solo albums over the past 20 years (not to mention jams with Woven Skull and Tomuttontu) with a considered approach to what lies just beyond her home; typically drawing on her attentive reading of the rural soundsphere to transmute the poetry of birdsong and the natural world into expressive musical metaphor.

The low bowed cello tone of regular spar Eimear Reidy underlines and opens out a breezy space where where the fiddle and violinists criss-cross air in reserved melodic flight and plucky figures that alternate like the play of light on Ireland’s remote North West. The piece unfolds to boggy pockets of percussion and passages of barely-there, hushed gloam, as though the wind itself was generating the players’ gestures, which rise to cloud castle hover around the midway, only to depart for Nyahh label boss Willie Stewart’s rolling drum thunder and scrape of Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh's fiddle rooted in the rolling landscape. Ultimately the folk soul of the turf rises in its final section, resembling a rousing, swaying folk song voiced by the strings in ideally creaky discord.

items.body:
Songs Before Bed (2022),  Otto Benson’s first physical release under his own name, following earlier work under aliases including Memo Boy, OTTO, and Pudding Club.

"Originally published as a digital-only release through Otto's own WNOADIARWB website and platforms on New Year's Eve 2022, Songs Before Bed bridges the gap between the more experimental psychedelic electronic works of OTTO and his most recent release, the acclaimed Peanut, released on NYE 2025. Blending brief pop fragments with melodic bedroom guitar, droning ambient shoegaze textures, and blissful IDM jaunts reminiscent of the Rephlex catalog, the album offers a seamless overview of Otto Benson's genre-defying sound. Originally conceived as a late-night record, Songs Before Bed (2022) rewards listening at any hour."

items.body:
Cloud-seeding dub techno sorcery x Rhythm & Sound worship by Stephen Hitchell’s cult cv313 and Radius projects, recorded in the heart of Detroit and preserved for posterity by Pole’s faithful remasters at Scape Berlin.

Echospace co-pilot Stephen Hitchell mans the cockpit solo on six sterling examples of Motor City dub techno purism within the 1st volume of ‘Altering Illusions’. His hallucinatory, synaesthetic tekkerz are in palpable effect from the damp bass thru to its noctilucent synth haze, bathing bodies in blissed-out arrangements that unfold up to 20 minutes in length, as with the echoes of BC’s ‘radiance’ registered in expansive parting piece ‘standing still’, and dredged up from drizzly depths on the cv313 rewire of Radius’ ‘Interpolation Tapes’.

Clubs are in the rearview for an 80 min trip deep under the hood of Echospace’s classic sound, fathoming deepest levels of sunken subs and elemental attrition on ‘i s i s’, and hingeing on Rhythm & Sound’s skankers' templates in ‘hypnosphere’ and mesmerising metallic resonance of ‘irradiate’, while ‘above clouds’ rises above the weather system into clearer, blue-skied dub techno lushness; think post-storm Lake Erie panoramas diffused by Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS.

items.body:
Derek Bailey, Loren Connors and Bill Orcutt fiends will be in their element with Nathan Roche’s 2nd salvo of experimental twangers for a resurrected Celluloid; the legendary label with roots in post-punk & NYC mutations, who would also  issue ‘The Lambada’ - the biggest selling global single of ’89.

Hailing to France, via Townsville, North east Queensland, and Sydney, Australia, Nathan Roche has carved out an uncompromising catalogue of guitar abstractions since the ‘00s with myriad outfits, including turns on Siltbreeze, London’s World of Echo, and France’s excellently titled Gone With The Weed label.

After helping reboot the Celluloid label with his very psych-garage-rock LP ’35 Rue du Théâtre’ in 2025, the dozen succinct bits of ‘aa in reverse’ mark a sharp departure from the classic composure of his previous works, and into fractious deconstructions of blues guitar vernacular, very much in the vein of iconoclasts, Derek Bailey, Bill Orcutt, or Tetuzi Akiyama, but accented with his own twang.

In this abstract blues mode Nqthqn reserves the right to really jangle and pluck the listener’s nerves in tart, prickly expressions that favour microtonality and dissonance over more consonant, Western pleasures. The warp and weft of his material snags from the off with the distended notes of ‘astra’ thru the rudely detuned mix elegance and grunt in ‘aa’, pulling into Loren Connors-esue midnight melancholy on ‘aka’ and relatively stretching out into 3 mins of curdled to finely melodic chops on ‘adversary’.

items.body:
All killer, no filler trotters from a golden period of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry’s foundational work at fabled studio, The Black Ark.

This 3rd in a prized series spies the wee madman conjuring multidimensional spectres from vocal recordings of regular spars: Max Romeo, The Jolly Brothers, Leroy Sibbles, The Mistic, and Devon Irons. Perry’s visionary, innovative application of studio-as-instrument tekkerz come to the fore in the music’s layered diffusions, which we may take for granted in contemporary music, but was radical back then, and whose uncanny appeal has only steeped with age. 

Including a solo standout in the ghostly, harmonised roots wooze of his ‘Dread Lion’ gem as King Scratch, it spans the signature, lysergic sparkle of his ‘Conscious Man’cut with The Jolly Brothers, thru a stepping 12” mix of Max Romeo’s ‘Norman’ (1978), and heat-hazed sway to Leroy Sibbles’ ‘Garden of Life’, along with The Mistic’s eyes-down devotional ‘Forward With Jah’, and sloshing nyabingi of ‘When Jah Comes’ for Devon Irons.

items.excerpt: Late, great Finnish maverick Mika Vainio’s debut ’94 minimal techno masterpiece, originally conceived as Ø, is treated to a much needed reissue, newly expanded with all tracks from the CD on vinyl for the first time and including the absolute all-timer ‘Lasi’ - 100% unmissable if you know what’s good. Back in circulation 20 years square since the 1st vinyl edition, and just over 30 years since the CD, ‘Metri’ serves a stone cold but heart-melting reminder of Mika’s way with puristic electronics.
items.body:
Late, great Finnish maverick Mika Vainio’s debut ’94 minimal techno masterpiece, originally conceived as Ø, is treated to a much needed reissue, newly expanded with all tracks from the CD on vinyl for the first time and including the absolute all-timer ‘Lasi’ - 100% unmissable if you know what’s good.

Back in circulation 20 years square since the 1st vinyl edition, and just over 30 years since the CD, ‘Metri’ serves a stone cold but heart-melting reminder of Mika’s way with puristic electronics. All 15 tracks from the CD are now cut to vinyl for a definitive edition of Mika’s exemplary solo statement, which would arrive the same year as his debut with Pan Sonic (the ‘Panasonic’ EP). It would dovetail with a time when the original Chicago, NYC and Detroit house and techno templates were being morphed in translation by new waves of artists such as Mika and his pal Ilpo Väisänen, or the likes of Richie Hawtin or Dan Bell, who all effectively streamlined the tekkerz of DJ Pierre, Blake Baxter and Rob Hood to even more stringent levels. 

What distinguishes Mika’s debut as Ø from all of the above is his feel for frosted tone and edge-of-distortion bite, rendered wth resounding plangency; all perhaps stereotypically reflective of his subarctic climes and expressing a sonic personality that would come to define certain strands of electronic music for decades to come, before his untimely passing in 2017, and ever since. We’ve lost count of the times the breathtaking motif of ‘Lasi’ has prompted us to a heads-down, air-punching jack, and reduced rooms at the afters to wide-eyed silent awe, until someone has to ask for an ID. 

Along with the likes of body-bouncing pulse and mind-bending acid tone to ‘Kuvio’ and ‘Twin Bleebs’, the uncanny amniotic ambience of ‘Radio’ and border-watch ambient tension of ‘Kenttä’, or the prototypes for his pure noise works in the ‘JL-CSG’, thru the sublime tension of ‘Dayak’, it’s every bit the ultra classique and we envy anyone coming across this album for the first time. Like many others, we will be taking the opportunity to replace well worn copies with a freshie to rinse and repeat for decades to come.

Seriously this one’s going to the grave with us.

items.body:
Barcelona-based Argentine sound artist Dima uses mythology to re-examine her personal world on 'Salva', dissolving instrumental phrases with confounding granular processes and allowing fragile trip-hop-inspired songs to emerge from the ambiance.

There's an unexpected balance on 'Salva'. At first, on the opener 'SOELAR' or its breathy follow-up 'APOGEO', you might think you have it figured out, its atmospheric blend of plasticky flutes and sci-fi pads. But as the latter track hits its third act, something unexpected appears - Dima's voice was already there, haunting the soundscape, but when a slowed-down beat joins it provides a real surprise. And 'Salva' keeps rocking from side to side, never settling into a reliable groove. On 'QUANTUM', Dima sings into an echoing void almost unaccompanied, but on 'FOLDING INWARD', she adds atmospheric synths and gong-y resonances to go in another direction, moving away from song structure towards grim abstraction. 

And after the one-two punch of the album's poppiest tracks, 'REACH' and 'IT HAD TO BURN', Dima concludes with 'Inked', a throbbing dark ambient nightmare that seems to dive deep beneath an alien ocean. Terrifying stuff.

items.body:
Steel-forged industrial brutalism from the Brum blast furnace of HALT, earning their Downwards stripes with a label debut that revels in dread tension and Midlands gloom somewhere between Scorn, Antonym, Karl O’Connor.

‘Slag Anthems’ cements Nathan Shwalbe & Craig Earp’s duo to the Downwards firm after Regis summoned them to the label’s 30th anniversary show at Birmingham’s Central, hosted amid familiar rogues; Surgeon, Russell Haswell, Mick Harris, Antonym and more. The specially packaged slab of heck builds on the solid foundations of 2020’s ‘Memory Fields’ LP for Erbium Records with a concentrated show of strength oozing from emulsified subs to plangent brutalist sound architecture, largely avoiding any regular drum patterns in favour of hulking offbeat structures and hallucinatory spectral silhouettes.

The duo’s native Brum is a presence and aesthetic muse throughout, prompting them to clash bin lids like duelling scimitars over pure bass effluence on ’Sassenach’, and lace their thrumming subs with a shiver of melodic glory on ‘Black Car’, or pull it all right down into Scorn-type mire on the recoiling drum play of ‘Rift Cantata’. A certain atmospheric levity to ‘Chernozem’ keeps it teetering just above an abyss they toe with macabre alacrity on ‘Pillars’, playing to a balance of black humour and uncompromising grit they tuck where the sun don’t shine on ‘I was just pleased to see you’.

Heavy.

items.body:
Chicago’s excellent, shapeshifting Kino Disk chase 8004’s ace dub abstractions with Eustress’ actions in familiar meadows of overgrown FX, farming post-dub techno landscapes highly tipped FFO Vladislav Delay, Echospace, False Aralia.

Peripheral to the Windy City’s fecund undergrowth, Indianapolis-based Heath Gillespie aka Eustress practises forms of dub techno at gauzy arm’s reach from the OG source. On the six tracks of ‘Exit’, his 2nd release for the label, he distorts familiar tropes to taste, diffusing a palette of windswept dub chords and unanchored bass in space crackling with an iridescent grayscale filament. 

His approach broadly swerves dub techno’s club momentum in favour of soothing meditation, letting everything hang out and slosh, loosely suspended in gritty yet lush amniotic plasm with an effect calling to mind the etheric depths of Echospace or even Werkbund’s atmospheric enigmas.

A hands-on background as mixing engineer comes to the fore in his work’s sensory tactility, convecting minds from a slow tempest to beatific bliss-out, rumbles of distant dub chord thunder and carpet rolling gouch-out, ultimately stranding up on the 8 min peninsula of ‘Exit 6’, under a borealis play of smudged, harmonised light, nerves combed into the breeze.

items.body:
Japan’s classic knack for slick jazz emulation is in debonaire effect on The Milky Way’s 1979 suite of bossanova and elegant city pop, produced by guitarist Makoto Matsushita and ambient pioneer Yasuaki Shimizu. Last available on LP 10 years ago, now trading for triple figures 2nd hand…

“Wewantsounds is delighted to present the first official reissue of the highly sought-after 1979 classic, Summer-Time Love Song by The Milky Way. Originally released on the Seven Seas label in Japan and produced by the legendary Makoto Matsushita—the visionary behind the cult masterpiece First Light —the album is a premier example of the sophisticated sound that defined the era. Featuring the cream of Japanese musicians, including Yasuaki Shimizu, the record offers a superb mix of AOR, jazz fusion, funk, and bossa nova. Remastered for vinyl by Colorsound Studio, this deluxe reissue features the original artwork, an 8 page booklet with a new introduction by Paul Bowler.”

items.body: Bassist Alexander Frangenheim and saxophonist Stefan Keune belong to the third generation of European Improvised Music (or fourth, depending on how you calculate). I came across Keune and his trio with bassist Hans Schneider and drummer Achim Krämer with No Comment (FMP 2009), Frangenheim was on my radar because he was a member of Cecil Taylor’s Workshop Band ( Legba Crossing , FMP 1988) and later on he released several very good recordings on the Creative Sources label. Their musical style - not atypical for European Improv in the 1990s and 2000s - was more abstract than the recordings of the godfathers of this music which - while experimental - were often very concrete. Whereas concrete improvisation works with direct, tangible materials, situations, or predetermined rules - be they small melodies, energetic structures, or even a pure desire for destruction (one need only think of Peter Kowald’s and Peter Brötzmann’s “Kaputtspiel” phase - even if the latter disliked the term), abstract improvisation detaches itself from external circumstances to express feelings or states of mind primarily through sound, structure, and form. Abstractions are evident in many ways on New Traces , Frangenheim’s and Keune’s debut collaboration as a duo: first, in the pauses - moments of silence that are repeatedly interspersed among the music’s hectic passages, as in “New Traces 1” or “New Traces 7” - and second, in the music’s extreme density and concentration. Both musicians employ extended playing techniques such as harmonics, overtones, and percussive strokes. It’s not about melodies, but about exploring timbres, textures, and dynamic extremes. Ultimately, however, the abstract moments are most evident in the frenzied runs and competing trills, the contrasts in register (especially in “New Traces 4“, where they really reach the limit of what listeners can bear to hear), the impetuous stylistic drive, and the simultaneous clarity of the sound. True, Keune still hisses, coos, hums, and gurgles for all he’s worth, and Frangenheim scrubs away, making his bass weep and crash - yet it’s as if one had stripped Barry Guy & Mats Gustafsson’s Sinners, Rather Than Saints (No Business, 2009) of all its embellishments, oriental flourishes, vibratos, frills and obvious crescendos (don’t get me wrong, I love this album) - to draw a concrete example for comparison. Just listen to “New Traces 8“. Here, the improvisation takes unpredictable turns and surprising sounds are created, yet the structure of the piece remains crystal clear. A prerequisite for this is that both musicians have such an excellent technique that during the more frenzied moments, instrumental timbres coalesce without getting in one’s way. The album is a treat for fans of abstract music and sonic exploration. Very recommended. New Traces is available as a download. new traces by Frangenheim / Keune Email This BlogThis! items.body:
YOASOBI are taking things to stadium scale. The Japanese duo, comprising producer Ayase and vocalist Ikura, will return to Singapore for the YOASOBI 10-CITY DOME & STADIUM TOUR 2026–2027 超惑星 ‘SUPER PLANET’ on 20 February 2027, taking over the Singapore National Stadium from 7 PM.

The concert will be the tour's only Southeast Asian stop and will make YOASOBI the first Japanese artist to headline the 55,000-capacity venue. The 10-city tour, their biggest international tour to date, will span five cities in Japan and five across Asia, including Singapore, Taipei, Seoul, and Hong Kong.

The upcoming show follows YOASOBI's sold-out Singapore concerts at Resorts World Sentosa and the Singapore Indoor Stadium. Known for hits including 'Yoru ni Kakeru' and 'Idol', the duo have also brought their music to international festival stages such as Coachella.

Tickets will be available via a Trip.com pre-sale on 18 August (10 AM to 11:59PM), followed by the general sale on 19 August (12 PM). Singapore-exclusive merchandise, collaborations, and fan activities are also set to be announced closer to the concert.

items.body:
Amsterdam electronic music institution Dekmantel is heading to Southeast Asia for the first time, teaming up with Desa Potato Head Bali for a one-day takeover in Seminyak.

Set for 26 September, the collaboration will bring a full day of electronic music and cultural programming to Potato Head Beach Club and Klymax, culminating in a night party headlined by Avalon Emerson, who will also make her Southeast Asian debut.

The takeover comes after years of exchanges between the Dekmantel and Potato Head teams. Dekmantel founder Casper van Tielrooij and Interstellar Funk's Olf van Elden have previously spent time in Bali, while the Potato Head team has visited Amsterdam for Dekmantel Festival.

Joining Avalon Emerson on the bill are Dekmantel Soundsystem, Fafi Abdel Nour, Ogazón, Soichi Terada, Danny Satria, Archie, Bagvs, Dita, Kaazi, Kiwed, and Sattle, bringing together artists from Europe, the US, Japan, and Indonesia.

The programme will stretch beyond the dancefloor, with daytime listening sessions, live Q&As, and a Desa Dialogue centred on ideas, culture, and creativity. The festivities will then move into the night across Potato Head Beach Club and Klymax.

The event will also spotlight artists from Bali and Indonesia, including Danny Satria, Dita, Kiwed, and Sattle. Archie and Bagvs will team up for a B2B set spanning deep house, minimal techno, spaced-out disco, and beyond, while Danny Satria will perform live.

Japan's Soichi Terada will also present his live set, while Dekmantel Soundsystem will reunite van Tielrooij and Olf van Elden behind the decks.

"It started as a friendship. We've spent years visiting each other, sharing music, sharing spaces, and now we get to share Bali with them," shared Potato Head resident DJ Dita. "It feels like the most natural thing! And also very much overdue."

The event will conclude with Avalon Emerson, whose sets move across house, techno, new wave, disco, and deep rave, closing out Dekmantel's first outing in Southeast Asia.

Tickets can be purchased here.

items.body:
Regina Song is gearing up for a milestone show. The Singaporean singer-songwriter will stage her first-ever headline concert in Singapore with everland: the launch show on 15 November at Capitol Theatre.

The concert will trace Regina's musical journey over the past two years, spanning songs from her debut album fangirl to her sophomore record everland. Inspired by Alice in Wonderland, everland marks a new sonic direction for the pop artist, with the upcoming show set to bring its whimsical world to the stage.

Fellow Singaporean singer-songwriter rhyu will support the show.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Regina Song (@sleepyreggy)

Regina has steadily built an audience across the region with her infectious pop hooks and songwriting centred on modern girlhood. Her track 'the cutest pair' went viral in late 2024, while fangirl has since amassed more than 65 million streams on Spotify and landed her at the top of Spotify's Viral 50 - Global playlist. She currently has over 600,000 monthly listeners.

The singer has previously appeared at Singapore events including Let's Celebrate 2025, Singapore Night Festival, Esplanade Red Dot, and SCAPE Music Day Out. She has also opened for grentperez and Matt Maltese. In January 2025, Regina embarked on her first sold-out Southeast Asia tour, making stops in Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Jakarta, and Manila.

Tickets for everland: the launch show will go on artist presale via SISTIC and the SG Culture Pass website on 18 August at 11 AM. Early Bird sales will run from 19 August at 11 PM until 26 August at 11 PM.

Ticket details are as follows:

Cat 1 VIP: S$198 / Early Bird S$188

Cat 1 Standing: S$98 / Early Bird S$94

Cat 2 Balcony: S$128 / Early Bird S$118

Priority entry add-on for Cat 1 Standing: S$30

VIP ticket holders will receive priority entry, a 1:1 photo with Regina, a signed poster, and merchandise. Fans can also use SG Culture Pass credits to offset ticket costs.

items.body:
Japanese pop-rock band OFFICIAL HIGE DANDISM have sold out their upcoming Singapore concert — but fans who missed out on tickets can still join in on the Higedan festivities.

Ahead of their sold-out OFFICIAL HIGE DANDISM ASIA TOUR 2026 – Singapore show on 21 August at The Star Theatre, the band will open a limited-time pop-up store at 313@Somerset from 15 to 23 August.

Part of the OFFICIAL HIGE DANDISM 2026 ASIA POP-UP, which will also make stops in Seoul, Taipei, and Bangkok, the Singapore edition will feature more than 20 merchandise items alongside exclusives made especially for the city.

Singapore-exclusive items include a T-shirt priced at SGD 65, a poster at SGD 14, and an LED magnet at SGD 19. Fans can also pick up a folding umbrella, beach towel, bandana, card wallet, strap pouch, key cap keyring, LP coasters, random keychains, tote bags, concert posters, and more.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Official髭男dism (@officialhigedandism)

The pop-up will additionally stock OFFICIAL HIGE DANDISM LIVE at STADIUM 2025 on DVD, Blu-ray, and CD.

Adding to the experience is an OFFICIAL HIGE DANDISM × PHOTOISM collaboration running from 1 August to 30 September. Exclusive photo frames will be available in each Asia tour city, giving Singapore fans another tour-specific keepsake.

The pop-up arrives as Higedan gear up for their first Singapore concert. In a statement, the band shared their excitement about meeting local fans: “We are incredibly excited to bring our music to Singapore for the first time.”

The group have also released their latest single, 'Stardust', accompanied by a new music video. It follows 'Make Me Wonder', the opening theme for anime series THE DARWIN INCIDENT.

Formed in 2012, Higedan are also known for songs including 'Pretender', 'Cry Baby' from Tokyo Revengers, and 'Mixed Nuts' from SPY x FAMILY. The band have amassed more than 10 billion cumulative streams and previously became the first Japanese act to receive “Japan’s Artist of the Year” at the Apple Music Awards.

items.body:
NCT 127 are giving fans another taste of their upcoming seventh studio album. Ahead of the release of BLINGY, the K-pop group unveiled a track video for 'Piñata', one of nine songs set to appear on the record.

'Piñata' sees NCT 127 bringing rock and hip-hop together, driven by electric guitar riffs, a funky bass groove, breakbeats, and a guitar solo. The track also features commanding rap chants, with its lyrics channelling the group's confidence in turning the stage into a celebration.

Its accompanying video takes that energy to the streets of Seoul after dark, with the members taking on the roles of streetwise fixers as they speed through the city.

Before BLINGY arrives, NCT 127 are also set to headline KCON LA 2026 on 14 August in Los Angeles.

The group will then mark the album's release with the NCT 127 7TH ALBUM [BLINGY] COMEBACK LIVE PARTY on 25 August at 8 PM KST. Taking place at Hall 10A of KINTEX Exhibition Center 2 in Ilsan, Korea, the event will feature performances of new material alongside conversations and behind-the-scenes stories from the making of the record.

BLINGY will be released on 24 August at 6 PM KST across global streaming platforms. The nine-track album includes its title track 'Blingy' as well as 'Piñata'. Pre-orders for the physical album are now available through online and brick-and-mortar retailers worldwide.

items.body:
The rush for BIGBANG tickets in Singapore is well underway — and fans are facing massive virtual queues and soaring third-party booking fees.

Tickets for BIGBANG's XX: COSMOS concert in Singapore on 17 October began rolling out with the official VIP membership pre-sale on 11 August. According to CNA Lifestyle, the virtual queue crossed 300,000 on its first day, while checks across fan groups and social media saw some queue numbers exceeding 500,000.

The VIP membership pre-sale eventually sold out at around 3:30 PM.

The huge demand has also driven up prices for third-party Help-To-Buy (HTB) services. According to The Straits Times, some providers are charging between S$110 and S$750 to help fans secure tickets, on top of official ticket prices.

HTB services essentially act as personal ticket shoppers, joining online queues and attempting to purchase tickets on a fan's behalf. Customers are typically refunded if the service is unsuccessful.

One HTB provider attributed the higher rates to the volume of users competing for tickets and the technological infrastructure required during the sale. Another pointed to BIGBANG's longtime fanbase — many of whom are now working adults — as well as the scarcity of having only one Singapore date announced so far.

Resale listings have also begun surfacing. The Straits Times reported that shortly after the VIP pre-sale opened, one Carousell listing offered a pair of VIP Diamond tickets, originally priced at S$458 each, for S$3,000.

BIGBANG's Singapore concert will mark the group's first performance in the country in a decade. G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung last performed together in Singapore during their Made VIP fan meeting tour in 2016.

The trio are also gearing up to release their new single, 'Biiig', on 19 August, their first release since 'Still Life' in 2022.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AEG Presents Asia (@aegpresentsasia)

Their XX: COSMOS world tour will kick off with three nights at Goyang Stadium in South Korea from 21 to 23 August, before heading to cities across the United States, Europe, and Asia.

Tickets to BIGBANG's Singapore show are priced from S$158 to S$498.

‘I Never Tell Anybody That The Music Is Meditative’: Arooj Aftab On Genre, Exotification & Her Bonobo Collaboration

12 August 2026

I know I am close to offending Arooj Aftab into disinterest. I have sidelined the bulk of the influences that go into her sound and, for three questions straight, have focused on investigating where and when the NYC-based Pakistani-American artist chose to draw on classical music.

“I wouldn't say that it's classical music. You can tell that I'm from a South Asian region when you listen to my music,” she corrects me, not for the first time but now more firmly. “But you can't really say, 'oh it sounds like she's classically trained.' It definitely doesn't sound like that.”

I am not the first music writer to hear classical music in her work. Whether branded neo-sufi or through allusions to Hindustani classical music and ragas, Arooj is frequently, if not near-constantly, associated with traditional styles or their adjacent forms – from her first record, 2014’s ‘Bird Under Water’, to her latest, ‘Night Reign’, released a decade later. Not without reason.

In the very first minute of the first track off her first album, Arooj’s discography begins with the kind of melodic interpolation over a single repeated word, “Maula” (the word for divine), most associated with khayal singing before breaking into the rest of the sufi poem ‘Mann Kunto Maula’, later going on to tackle the popular thumri ‘Aey Na Balam’. Even her breakout track ‘Mohabbat’ (which made Arooj the first Pakistani to win a Grammy and was publicly favourited by Barack Obama) from 2021’s ‘Vulture Prince’ is a ghazal popularised by the likes of Mehdi Hassan and Farida Khanum.

Arooj Aftab

There is no dearth of people combining jazz with contemporary electronica or even with Hindustani classical music. While it is easy to see how the former two styles seep into the expression of this Berklee-trained polymath who has worked as a producer on film and video games, it is the addition of that third language that separates Arooj from the rest of the jazz-with-something canon. More precisely, her ability to shed some of the weighty layers and technical density without losing the emotional core. The elaborate melodic flights of jazz or Hindustani classical singing become, in her hands, phrases that can be casually sung alongside the work of the most popular singer-songwriters.

“We're still very genre-oriented and want to pin it down,” she says. “People really, journalists mostly – and especially when you are introducing a new style of music – they want you to figure out some way to define it so people can understand.”

She recalls the early days, around the release of her 2014 debut album, when people reacted to the music with curiosity. She had to participate in how people talked about her music, the language around it and how it was framed. But more than a decade later, things are different. Her audience now stretches across the world, with listeners from South Asia, Detroit and places far beyond receiving her music with a similar mixture of familiarity and surprise – familiarity with the sounds they grew up with, and surprise at the ones they did not expect to hear beside them. “It really draws them in, as if they've heard this before, but they'll also be drawn in, in a way that they're a little surprised and a little intrigued. Because there are parts of it that they have not. And that is really exciting. That combination!”

Her protest at having her multifaceted sound reduced to its traditional South Asian influences isn’t unfounded. “I've always been someone who crosses the genres, you know? It is just as much American as it is Pakistani or as it is South Asian,” she continues. “It's all very rooted in my personal journey.” If there is ghazal or thumri in her discography, then so are jazz standards (like her rendition of ‘Autumn Leaves’ on 2024’s ‘Night Reign’). There is an entire modular synths-led ambient-experimental album in her discography: 2018’s ‘Siren Islands’. Yet these aren't necessarily the elements through which Arooj has come to be recognised on the global stage.

“The exotification of South Asian music comes in so many forms, but I don't think my music really allows for it,” she says, citing and amusingly demonstrating some of the easier targets: ragas being warbled over dance tracks played at European raves, Buddha Bar music, or the kind you’d find in a stereotypical Boston yoga studio. “It by itself rejects that and asks for something – asks to be taken seriously and asks to be a part of modern music without these tropes.”

She doesn’t outright reject the presence of the sounds rooted deep in her culture; rather, she doesn’t see them as anything too distinct to be given more attention than any of the other musical influences.

Growing up in a music-loving family, first in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and later in Lahore, Pakistan, Bade Ghulam Ali Khan, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and Abida Parveen were just as much part of her musical upbringing as Billie Holiday and Mariah Carey. Not in the sense of formal music training, but as records always playing in family gatherings with friends or without. “I grew up with that just like as if it was the curtains in the house”, she explains, recalling memories such as that of her parents being obsessed with Jagjit Singh and Chitra for a phase. “I never really had consciousness of: right now I’m doing jazz, and right now I’m doing South Asian. The identity of both was always very intertwined. It wasn’t very divisive in my brain.”


Bonobo (left) and Arooj Aftab walk on one of the trails at the Broken Arrow Ranch in Woodside

She wasn’t thinking about genres either when she reached out to the British electronica giant Simon Green, better known as Bonobo. She was simply interested in bringing out more of what already existed within her. “It doesn't always have to be so sombre, you know?” she says. “There's a side of me that isn't sombre. There's a side of me that is very fun and very unserious, and I want to explore that through music too!”

So, she reached out to Green, another artist whose music has been part of her life. “Is anyone from my generation not a huge Bonobo fan?” she offers, pointing to Green among dance music artists whose most club-focused tracks still carry considerable emotional depth. She initially reached out to him to remix a track from ‘Night Reign’. Instead, he invited her to create together for his new album.

A year later, she joined him in the secluded California town of Woodside, where he was working on his album at Neil Young’s Broken Arrow Ranch studio. When she arrived, she already had poetry, both in English and Urdu, which she was working on for her own upcoming album. Some written by herself, some by friends and some by other inspirations. The pair began developing two or three ideas, one of which eventually became ‘Fire on the Water’, a lead single from Bonobo’s upcoming work ‘Distance in Static’.

“The writing process is always like, neither has a head nor a tail,” she says, recalling trying the song’s melody and lyrics (by friend Yasra Rizvi) around fire and desire on a different idea that wasn’t working together. The pair shelved it and moved on. One evening, after a lunch and a walk through the redwood-surrounded town, Bonobo started fiddling with an acoustic guitar loop he had recorded while testing a studio input.

“I was like, WAIT... this beat is inviting something. The fire on the water will work here,” she continues. “So I started weaving it in, line by line, and he started playing that guitar riff. We had this astonishing, hushed excitement as we kept putting the pieces together because we could feel that we were making something very special.” Bonobo felt the same, echoing later how the moment the song happened is when he could first see the album taking shape.

It’s a repeating loop and the percussive pulse of the track alongside the glitchy micro-grooves until the drums enter halfway through. Over them, Arooj sustains her phrases until they relent into quick stops, as cinematic strings join her in harmony. The drums, upright bass-like synth tone and plucked guitar do suggest a jazz palette but never enter that territory. There are none of the melodic interpolations borrowed from khayal singing that get singled out when discussing Arooj’s work. None of the tropes that people like me tend to reach for, save for the Urdu lyricism that cursory listeners might get hung up on. Instead, the repetitions, the sustained notes, the micro elements combine into a defining tranquil bed that neither musician would be immediately associated with, yet feels entirely natural to both.

I call it meditative at first, another descriptor assigned to her frequently, and run into a correction yet again.

"I never tell anybody that the music is meditative," she says. "I mean, they say transcendental, ambient, meditative – those markers definitely join my name and my music a lot. And I guess it is, right? I don't know. When I listen to music to meditate, I wouldn't put on my music. I wouldn't put on 'Raat Ki Rani' or 'Mohabbat'. How can you meditate to that? It feels insane to me."

Ambient-influenced, then? One more word, one more attempt.

"I don't even think it is ambient. It's a little bit too busy for that," she says, contemplating it without seeming entirely sure. The word conjures more drone music for her, with long safe bansuri phrases, or hokey new age chants that keep their purpose on the surface.

I don't offer a third.

"It's okay. They can call it whatever they want," she says. "I'm just going with the vibes, you know? And I'm also not pushing back."

Except once.

"If anyone starts calling it like, chant music, I will probably push back." She laughs at that thought. "I'm not going to make that mistake."

.

.
.

Words: Amaan Khan

items.body: Structura Parva — literally “small structure” — acts as both title and manifesto. Seven years after Forma, the Italian duo Filtro (Luca de Biasi and Angelo Bignamini) have moved away from long-form improvisations built from concrete sounds and electrical interference towards something more concentrated, deliberate, and architectural. Across six concise pieces, they construct miniature sonic ecosystems from the sparsest of materials, embracing self-imposed limitations as catalysts for invention. Working with only a handful of sounds per track, Filtro adopt an approach reminiscent of Oulipo’s creative constraints, treating composition as a process of exploring the possibilities contained within a tightly defined framework. Yet the result never feels academic. The sounds themselves remain stubbornly alive: intermittent clicks, fragile drones, processed acoustic fragments and high-frequency traces evolve, misbehave and interact in ways that resist predictable looping or repetition. Rather than expanding ideas through scale, Filtro trace how small gestures ripple through space, giving the EP a sense of depth and movement. What distinguishes Structura Parva is its refusal of sonic flattening. Every sound retains its material presence and tactile character, whether emerging from a sampler, field recordings or processed everyday objects. The duo’s attention to dynamics and spatial placement ensures that even the sparsest passages feel animated by hidden tensions. These are not static minimal compositions but living structures, constantly shifting beneath the surface. The EP’s subtitle of sorts — “sounds for night reflections and dark disquiets” — feels apt. There is a subdued melancholy running throughout the record, but also curiosity and attentiveness. By reducing their palette and abandoning improvisation in favour of meticulous composition, Filtro have created their most focused work to date: a quietly compelling study in how much emotional weight can be carried by the smallest of structures. In the following interview Angelo Bignami and Luca de Biasi explain their working process. Structura Parva feels like a significant shift from the long-form improvisation for concrete sounds and electrical interferences of Forma towards much shorter and more concentrated pieces. What led you to embrace these “small structures”? Was this reduction a deliberate aesthetic decision or the natural outcome of your evolving practice? Luca de Biasi: After Forma, we took a long break to dedicate ourselves to our solo work, which also gave us the opportunity to reflect on what we wanted Filtro to become. The idea was to work meticulously on individual sounds, processing them and finding affinities with other sounds to shape the pieces. We set a strict limit: just two sounds each and nothing else. The biggest change for me was using a sampler, which allowed me to process sound differently than in the past and focus on individual sounds before looking at the whole picture. We also worked extensively on dynamics and the movement of sound in space. In some tracks, this remained direct, while in others we added the natural echoes of the different environments where we re-recorded the pieces. Angelo Bignamini: It was a bit of both. It represents an evolution of our sound, moving away from what were initially uncontrolled, improvisation-based impulses toward actual composition focused on a few core elements. I believe this shift was influenced by our shared listening habits at the time, as well as a mutual desire to produce something more focused and structured. The EP is described as reflecting a new approach to “minimal structures and small electronics.” What does “small electronics” mean for Filtro in practical and conceptual terms? Are you interested in intimacy, scale, fragility, or perhaps a different relationship between sound and space? L: The new approach was all about working on individual sounds before the whole composition. In practice, I used a modular synthesizer consisting simply of an oscillator, a complex envelope, and a filter, constantly tweaking the sound until I achieved a satisfactory result. I did the same using very simple field recordings. As I mentioned, the choice of individual sounds, their interaction, and their interconnectivity were the core ideas behind the project. A: It is called “small electronics” simply because the entire project is built on just a few elements—each track develops across two or three layers at most—and an extremely minimal setup. Often, we are just using everyday objects or small acoustic instruments, which we record and process using a sampler and a laptop. The core idea was to maximize the value of each individual sound and distribute it throughout the space, which inevitably transforms both its signifier and its signified. Both of you have long been interested in sound detached from its original context and meaning. On Structura Parva, the sounds often seem stripped down to traces, gestures and subtle interactions. How do you decide when a sound has been reduced enough, and how do you prevent minimalism from becoming merely an exercise in subtraction? L: For this latest project, each individual sound was developed separately by Angelo and me. We both worked on our own ideas without any prior agreement. After months of work, we decided it was time to meet up and listen to what we had done. Choosing which sounds to use was ultimately quite simple and quick. I don’t know how, but the work each of us had done seemed to share a common goal. A: Honestly, I didn’t really worry about that problem. The goal was simply to find minimal structures that could convey emotional meaning—which, in a way, is a prerequisite for any kind of music. There is almost always a rhythmic element, a background texture or drone, and a melodic element. If you look past the totally hallucinated style, we aren’t actually that far off from a traditional song structure. Angelo’s work frequently explores deterioration, tape processes and feedback, while Luca’s practice involves modular synthesis and improvisation. How has the dialogue between these approaches changed since Forma? Has the balance between improvisation and composition shifted over the years? L: Our approach has always been improvisational. We used to meet for long sessions and then extract the sections that would become the final work. This time, it was different: we worked on the tracks individually, then discussed them and decided together which parts made sense when combined. We then re-recorded them in various environments to give them depth. We also placed great importance on the movement of sounds in space. Therefore, this latest work is much more compositional than our previous ones. A: In this latest work, there is absolutely nothing improvised. We worked in perfect sync on the individual tracks, with each of us utilizing our own sounds and processing techniques. What united us was a shared vision to produce something simple and circular, yet containing an internal evolution driven primarily by how the individual layers intersect. Nothing was left to chance, except for the deliberate use of random modulations and stereophonic automation. The EP is presented as “sounds for night reflections and dark disquiets.” There is a strong sense of restraint and suspended tension throughout the six tracks. Were there particular emotional states, environments or listening situations that informed the album, or do you prefer to leave such associations entirely in the hands of the listener? L: There were certainly external factors that influenced the choice and development of the sound—not necessarily musical ones. In my case, books had a significant impact, changing my approach to life and, consequently, to music. Using a sampler also definitely allowed me to focus more on single sounds. However, I prefer not to give listeners any specific direction regarding our influences, so that their listening experience remains entirely unique and personal. A: The way people interpret tracks is one of the most incredible wonders of music. Because of that, I prefer to let listeners filter the pieces however they choose and place them in whatever context feels right to them. Personally, I feel these sounds express themselves best in a nighttime setting, but that is by no means a strict rule. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — One could say that everything was building up to the emergence of Starsailor, like the base of a massive pyramid tapering to a razor-sharp point, at once provocative and evocative, where Tim found the true meaning of his existence. Psychology speaks of the "primal scream" for good reason; sometimes, one must undergo a certain process, a cathartic one, perhaps, to reach one's destination. Tim Buckley's destiny lay in the stars, yet he had to get there by traveling a long road; folk and jazz guided him toward that atonal, distorted, avant-garde present where he built his sanctuary alongside his inseparable partner, Lee Underwood.In Come Here Woman, John Balkin played the bass furiously, while Lee Underwood experimented on guitar with dark, almost operatic flamenco-style melodies, and then Tim began to sing, as he never had before... and never would again. A singular shooting star that, if you didn't see or hear it... you missed it.Then the music kicks in, and you have to jump on board, it's rock 'n' roll, too; the percussion and guitar take on a jazzy, yet atonal, quality, as does the electric piano. It's all a storm that catches us by surprise, blink, and you'll miss it."I Woke Up," accompanied by the horns, feels like waves crashing against the beach sand and receding; the muted trumpet and double bass are the perfect companions. Tim's voice shifts, sometimes a tenor, other times higher-pitched, but it is always exactly right, creating a relaxed summer vibe even amidst this strange, dreamlike atmosphere. Throughout the album, we never quite know what time or place we inhabit, yet we know we are truly there."Monterey" is an acoustic rock track, with jazz undertones, where Tim's voice takes the place of the electric guitar and its solos. It features peaks and valleys, ranging from whispers to moments where his voice, striking a high note, sounds almost like a saxophone. He is like a Californian Peter Hammill; while Lee Underwood kept the guitar going with ceaseless repetition, it was Tim who handled the variations. Far from being chaotic improvisation, there was indeed chaos, yet it was a chaos driven by melody, moving perfectly toward its climax."Moulin Rouge" is a lovely interlude sung in French, showcasing the beautiful voice he was known for, accompanied by the trumpet. "Song to the Siren" and "Jungle Fire" represent two extremes of his vocal range, the former restrained yet outwardly expressive, the latter a long build-up culminating in an explosion alongside the band, where his voice truly functioned as just another instrument amidst wild, guttural, and primal improvisation. This trajectory leads to the title track, "Starsailor," which evokes a space-like atmosphere, one that feels as though it is tumbling into a black hole, featuring vocal stylings that range from Zappa-esque lows to Hammill-esque highs, yet serve a vastly different purpose; the mood steers the song toward a progressive sound, far removed from the jazz style found at the album's start.The Healing Festival revisits free jazz, pure double bass and saxophone, with Tim himself singing, stretching his voice and warping it like a rain-soaked blanket that changes shape once it's wet. "Down by the Borderline" ends with a flamenco flair, just as it began, but featuring the trumpet. Then the guitar kicks in with an unstoppable groove, joined by the drums and Tim, who is practically prancing with sheer delight just listening to them set the stage. He launches into the song with all his heart and lungs, following a syncopated rhythm; his vocal delivery is intentionally jagged, full of deliberate pauses and breaks, and in those gaps, a different path is paved: the path of Starsailor, his finest album, a record that could take him all the way up to the clouds, where it never rains.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The phrase "Changing Horses" has always evoked images for me of "turning the page," or a need to slow down and gain perspective, to view things from a different angle and perhaps clarify a change in direction. It feels like a self-imposed exercise in clarity. And I always sensed great wisdom in the music of this sixth album by The Incredible String Band, by then firmly established as a quartet.It begins quietly and without grand ambition with a country-tinged track called "Big Ted," which later shifts into a boogie style. "White Bird" feels almost like a recited poem, even though it is sung by Mike Heron, accompanied by flute, organ, and guitar, and that simplicity lends it a power... one that is further enhanced by the inclusion of the choir. Vocal layering was one of the band's strengths, and it is beautifully realized here. There is a moment where the track pauses, leaving just the guitar improvising notes'almost at random'and therein lies another kind of sonic power: out of nowhere, he finds a very specific, strong melody (which was undoubtedly already in his head) yet makes it seem spontaneous... seamlessly segueing into the next section of "White Bird."In addition to its catchy chorus, "Dust Be Diamonds" makes excellent use of the vibraphone and features instruments that mirror the melody during the chorus. "Sleepers, Awake!" is another example, one of the best, of their vocal harmonies, which conveyed not just musicality, but the harmony that reigned between them at the time. With nothing but their voices, they could reach both luminous and dark corners at will."Mr. and Mrs." is an evocative melody, intriguing and mysterious, featuring a touch of Bossa Nova guitar before shifting into a medieval sound, transporting the listener to the Druid forest that was their natural habitat. Out of nowhere, the tempo could quicken and take on a bluesy feel; that hippie spirit they embodied held layers and nuances, varying heights like the pines in a forest, just as their music could evolve, becoming psychedelic and even slightly funky at times, only to turn overwhelmingly simple and deeply moving."Creation" is the album's centerpiece; here, the band draws upon its most experimental Indian music roots, incorporating choir, percussion, sitar, and tabla, to offer a journey that literally transports the listener. This was another of the quartet's strengths, aided here by Ivan Pawle on organ and piano. It feels like witnessing an occult ritual, something meant for the few, perhaps even incognito, hidden away amidst the forest.When they chose to, they could display virtuosity, with the guitar accelerating to match the rhythm of the tabla, while the spoken-word vocals lend the track a prophetic air.The theme is creation, and every element is present: the chaos, that moment before form takes shape, like an incandescent mass of liquid lava that darkens as it cools and hardens into solid rock, all embodied by that choir and that endless sitar. Next comes a unique piano-driven section that shifts the very ground beneath one's feet (both back then and still today when listening to the record). Finally, the track gives way to a bluesy, tavern-style finish; the journey's circle was both completed and broken, and that was precisely the intention: to break the cycle in order to move forward. The future would bring the musical U and many more adventures.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Aether, created in 2021 by four friends, initially began as a project for bassist Andrea's final thesis, with the aim of moving away from conventional jazzy sounds. Their sound blends post-rock, contemporary classical rock, and multi-layered jazzy prog."Oort Cloud" is a prime example, fusing ambient, jazzy tones, and dino-tinged progressive rock reminiscent of King Crimson, with a flute buzzing here and there. A long, contemplative suite encourages a dreamlike journey, with a primal Fender Rhodes piano accompanying the oppressive psychedelic guitar riff. "Vogon" opens with Collins' electronic drums, then shifts to a jazzier feel with Claudio Milano's frenetic narration. The air soars on Zappa-esque jazz-rock guitar in the purest tradition, flirting with the great Return To Forever on the distinctive piano; a frenetic finale with infectious energy. "Five Shades, Four Frames" opens with a spacey sound, a prominent rhythmic bassline. A drift into hyperspace follows this encroaching Crimson-esque crescendo; improvisation steers clear of interstellar notes. Midway through, the sound takes on an Arabic quality, reminiscent of a Star Wars desert, over a psychedelic Tangerine Dream melody. The obvious jazzy Rhodes turn on a drumbeat with a hint of Steven Wilson is surprising."The Melancholy of the Little Prince" features a melancholic piano drifting over percussion and electronic notes, giving free rein to the fretless bass. Musical scales, a crackling, distorted sound as if from a parallel universe. "Panta Rei" sees the flute searching for its footing, wandering notes for a learned musical digression; jazz, unmistakably King Crimson, Andrea's guitar surfing avant-garde territory for a controlled jumble. Dynamic and apocalyptic with its explosive contemporary finale, "Swerve" opens with a snowy, religious, ethereal feel. The captivating keyboards lead into post-rock territory illuminated by scores reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. The track then veers into jazzy soft rock territory with a distinctive piano demon unleashing a fury, recounting the new Italian sound.Aether brilliantly dares to create a jazzy post-rock fusion, injecting a dose of ambient and modern prog, opening this movement to the contemporary world.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After debuting in 2021 with one of Brazil's strangest contributions to the world of zeuhl metal, theJo�o Pessoa based PAPANGU jettisoned the metallic edge of its debut "Holocene" with its follow up"Lampi�o Rei" which followed in 2024 with more of a classic progressive rock approach mixed with thesounds of Brazil ranging from forro, xaxado and udigrudi. The band returns with its Brazilianbravado cocktail of prog and local flavors with its third installment CELESTIAL which features a 10-track concept that once again steers its sound into a new direction. Trimming down from a sextet toa five-member outfit, CELESTIAL follows suit with the metal aspects deemphasized (although stillpresent) and more retro warmth evoked through the use of analog equipment and a passion for bringingthe likes of jazz fusion, symphonic prog, zeuhl and other classic prog influences to this Brazilianstreet party.Another main feature of this third musical expedition is that on CELESTIAL the vocals are ratherdownplayed with crafty instrumental complexities nurturing warm inviting melodies into displays ofprog majesty evoking the elegance of 70s jazz fusion, the artifice of Gentle Giant complexities andthe sneaky labyrinthine excursionist proclivities that nurtured intuited perspicacity throughmusical obstacle courses that never lose their soul and of course all fortified with the true joiede vie that only Brazilian musical styles can deliver. It's a triumphant return to a new form afterwhat sounded to me like a clunky and disjointed sophomore offering. More focused and refined,CELESTIAL may not deliver the supposed concept of a bandit on a mission to prevent an ecologicaldisaster in some undisclosed form but for what the story narrative lacks in heft, the musicalprowess more than compensates for.CELESTIAL may share an album title with the post-metal band Isis but delivers a truer musical vibeof heavenly bliss with the Rhodes piano and vintage keyboard sounds leading the way. Add someunexpected sound effects from a rubber chicken and Brazilian folk instruments and it's easy to getsucked into the majesty of CELESTIAL's intricate flow of modern modern meets retro with a sensiblerunning time of just over 50 minutes. The album's energy bursts into full gear on the opening "Mau-Olhado" and continues its journey of jubilee throughout the album's ten distinct installments. Awaft of classic Canterbury is present throughout evoking the warmth of that classic Egg / SoftMachine / Hatfield & The North along with occasional bursts of heavier rock that emulates blackmetal (at least in the vocal department) all creatively wrapped in the retro prog padding that keepsthe album amazingly well balanced.Tracks like "Fechamento de Corpo" exhibit the band's menagerie of modernity with staccato basedgrooves fortified with crazy contrapuntal effects and a zeuhl-esque propulsion system that allowsthe cadences and motifs to cozy up together snuggly like a den of hibernating mammals. While theprevious works had me wondering if PAPANGU was primarily a one hit wonder with its out of the gatecrashing the prog party debut, CELESTIAL puts those concerns to rest with a beautifully deliveredprocession of tones and timbres executed in crafty compositions that find the band a form ofmaturation that seemed to be lost on "Lampi�o Rei." Throughout this smorgasbord of retro prog onecan detect moments of classic Yes, Genesis, Gentle Giant, Weather Report, Egg and the list goes onhowever PAPANGU also ekes out modernities with excellent production value and 21st century jazzplaybook tricks. While the metal felt out of balance on the previous album, here the subordinateeffects are instigated perfectly without the bombast ruining the dynamic flow. A brilliant thirdalbum here!
